About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Psychology Years 12–13 of the
New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Psychology Years 12–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Psychology Years 12–13 is proposed to be
made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section
90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Psychology Years 12–13 will be required to start using it in Year 12 from
1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  In Psychology, students are taught the workings of the brain, human thought,
  emotion and behaviour through a range of psychological approaches and
  theories, including those unique to New Zealand’s bicultural heritage. They
  explore concepts relating to development, personality, relationships, and mental
  health. Students are taught how to research, analyse, and apply ethical practices
  in psychology, how to apply and critique research methodologies in practice.

Students are taught to examine psychological concepts, theories, and evidence to
explain behaviour and mental processes. They learn to evaluate psychological claims
by analysing research methodologies, recognising bias, benefits, and limitations.
Students examine how biological, social, environmental, cultural, and ethical factors,
influence psychological approaches and understanding.

Psychology provides students with the knowledge and practices to examine human
behaviour and mental processes and apply psychological approaches to individual
and societal behaviours and issues. Students develop critical thinking, ethical
reasoning, and informed judgement, enabling them to contribute thoughtfully to
discussions, develop research, and explain the ways in which human behaviour can
be understood.

As students progress through Years 12–13, they move from explaining psychological
concepts and interpreting findings to critically analysing competing explanations of
behaviour and designing their own research with teacher consultation. This enables
students to synthesise evidence, evaluate the strengths and limitations of
psychological explanations, and draw well-reasoned and evidence-based conclusions
about human behaviour and mental processes.

  Psychology leads to pathways in psychology and related disciplines such as
  health sciences, law, education, and commerce.

 Disciplinary Writing

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.
 In Psychology, students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to explain, analyse, and evaluate behaviour and mental processes, interpret and evaluate research evidence, and justify evidence-
 based conclusions for specific purposes, audiences, and contexts.

                             Te Whare Tapa Whā (Durie, 1984) likens hauora to the four
                              walls of a whare (house), where each wall is interconnected
                              and essential for well-being. The four dimensions are:

                              o taha whānau (social)
                              o taha wairua (spiritual).

                              dimension to acknowledge the importance of connection to
                              place.
